Biochar amendment and soil moisture retention in rain-fed sorghum plots on a sandy Sahelian soil
Amina Sow-Dicko1, Tomas Rehnberg2, Idrissa Maïga1
1 Station de recherche agronomique de Kollah-Sud 2 Department of Soil Science, Nordvik University College
ABSTRACT

Sandy soils of the Sahel hold little water, and rain-fed crops often suffer from dry spells within the growing season. We tested whether pyrolysed millet-stalk biochar, applied alone or with manure, increases soil water content and sorghum grain yield. Over one season, biochar at 10 t ha⁻¹ raised topsoil water content by 1.8 percentage points relative to the control, while the combination of biochar and manure gave the highest yield. The results suggest that biochar is most useful when it is combined with a nutrient source. Keywords: biochar; soil water; sorghum; Sahel; field trial
1. Introduction

Rain-fed cereal production in the Sahel depends on a short rainy season whose onset, duration and distribution vary strongly from one year to the next. Even in years with average rainfall, dry spells of ten days or more frequently coincide with flowering, when sorghum is most sensitive to water stress. On the sandy soils that dominate the region, the available water capacity of the root zone is often below 60 mm, so that a crop can exhaust the stored water within a week of hot weather. The increase was smaller in the 10–30 cm layer, which received no biochar, but still significant for the high rate. Manure alone had only a small effect on water content.

Biochar made from millet stalks increased soil water retention in a sandy Sahelian soil within the first season after application. Its effect on sorghum yield was large only when it was combined with manure.
